b: Back in September, the denizens of X were having a complete crash out over the idea that their chatbots might not be conscious. How could their new favorite toys not love them back? No lesser authority than Richard Dawkins pronounced them to be living after a few days of being love-bombed by one, as is their default behavior. Why, they were counting on them for companionship, maybe even physical affection one day in the near future to fulfill their dreams of a woman being nothing more than a prop for showing off their success. This was an affront to everything they held dear.

It is a question worth answering though, because it carries legal implications. If LLMs are capable of metacognition, that is, they know they exist as entities and adjust their thought processes on the fly because they’re self-aware, then we have to figure out if you can actually own an AI model, experiment with it, or deactivate it. We would need consent to do anything, and that consent would need to be informed, and how would we even know if we adequately informed an AI system of, well, anything?

But before we start debating how many digital angels are dancing on the pin of a RAM chip, we should probably establish if this is a real concern. Unfortunately, when you’re debating if chatbots are conscious, almost all the arguments from the yes camp boil down to “well, how do you know you’re not just meat doing statistics?” and then keep on begging the question. Instead of showing how an LLM attains self-awareness, they want you to spend time defending how you know you’re a conscious being capable of metacognition, often to an absolutely absurd extent.
